subject: chemistry
title: Chemical Kinetics Adventure 3: Arrhenius equation and catalysis
welcome_lead: Today you'll plot ln k vs 1/T and find Ea with the Arrhenius equation.
meta_desc: Chemistry HL — Arrhenius equation, ln k vs 1/T plot, catalysts, enzymes.
final_note: You learned k = Ae^(-Ea/RT), ln k = -Ea/RT + ln A gives a straight line with slope -Ea/R, and catalysts lower Ea by providing alternative pathways.

walkthroughs.body_html:
k = A · e^(-Ea/RT)

k = rate constant; A = pre-exponential factor (~frequency × geometry); Ea = activation energy; R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T in K.

Higher T → e^(-Ea/RT) ↑ → k ↑ → rate ↑.

Take ln: ln k = -Ea/R · (1/T) + ln A.

Plot ln k (y) vs 1/T (x):
- Slope = -Ea/R → Ea = -slope × R.
- Intercept = ln A.

Two-point version: ln(k₂/k₁) = -Ea/R · (1/T₂ - 1/T₁).

Catalysts lower Ea — and so dramatically speed reactions.

- Heterogeneous: Fe in Haber; Ni in hydrogenation; Pt in catalytic converters. Reactants adsorb on surface.
- Homogeneous: H⁺ in ester hydrolysis; transition metal complexes.
- Enzymes: lock-and-key/induced fit. Optimal T and pH.

International perspective: Haber-Bosch process (Germany 1909) feeds ~50% of world today — but uses ~2% of global energy.
